stories.title: Chicago/Midwest People & Company News, week of September 25, 2026
stories.excerpt: Daniel Management Group (DMG), a Chicago-based multifamily management and investment company, announced the promotion of Lauren Evett to vice president of property management. The promotion reflects Evett’s expanding role at DMG as she takes on a larger and more diverse portfolio spanning a wider array of assets, clients and staff. She has become an increasingly critical part of DMG’s leadership team, particularly in guiding properties through the demanding transition-to-stabilization period. T2 Capital Management announced the launch of Base Living, the firm’s wholly-owned, tech-enabled property management company. With the launch of Base Living, T2 welcomes Tyler Yates as director of property management, where he is responsible for operational and financial performance of T2’s property portfolio, ensuring high standards of service and maximizing returns. Yates manages Base Living’s 24 new team members across Illinois, Indiana, and Florida, and is supported by eight members of T2’s corporate team. He reports to Aaron Tink, Principal of T2, who oversees the firm’s asset management division and leads Base Living. Cushman & Wakefield has promoted Jack Goldsborough from director to senior director. Based in Kansas City, Goldsborough specializes in industrial sale and lease transactions throughout the Midwest, representing landlords, occupiers, investors and developers across a broad range of industrial real estate assignments. Over his 12-year commercial real estate career, Goldsborough has completed more than 300 transactions totaling over $500 million in value. Financial services veteran Kevin Christopher has joined Chicago-based Key Mortgage as senior vice president of mortgage production. Christopher brings 34 years of financial services experience, with an extensive background in mortgage lending and sales leadership to his new role at the independent lender that operates in multiple states. stories.title: KBS Acquires 26-Story Austin Office Tower
stories.excerpt: KBS completed the sale of 515 Congress, a 26-story, 267,956-square-foot Class A office tower at the corner of Congress Avenue and Sixth Street in downtown Austin, Texas. A joint venture of Palmatum Ventures, AQUILA and Glendon Capital Management acquired the property. JLL represented KBS in the transaction. 515 Congress was owned by KBS Real Estate Investment Trust III. Located in the heart of downtown Austin, 515 Congress is within walking distance of the Texas State Capitol and dining, retail, hotel and cultural amenities. During its ownership, KBS invested more than $15.5 million in capital and base-building improvements, including renovations to the lobby, tenant lounge and conference facilities and modernization of the elevators. JLL Capital Markets brokers Mike McDonald, Jonathan Napper, Ryan Stevens and Drew Fuller represented KBS in the sale of 515 Congress. The post KBS Acquires 26-Story Austin Office Tower appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: KBS sold 515 Congress, 26-story Austin office tower, to Palmatum/AQUILA/Glendon JV

stories.summary: KBS Real Estate Investment Trust III divested 515 Congress, a 267,956-sf Class A office tower at Congress Avenue and Sixth Street in downtown Austin, after investing $15.5 million in modernization. The property traded to a joint venture anchored by Palmatum Ventures, AQUILA, and Glendon Capital Management. JLL Capital Markets brokered the sale.
stories.impact: Office divestiture in downtown Austin reflects REIT capital rotation away from office; however, buyer consortium suggests institutional confidence in prime downtown Austin locations. Limited direct multifamily impact, but office-to-multifamily conversion potential exists if repurposing becomes necessary. Watch for multifamily demand in downtown Austin driven by tech/corporate expansion separate from office cycle.

The portfolio was purchased from LCN Capital Partners and the deal was brokered by Bryn Feller and Josh Dicker of Northmarq. Three of the properties are in Texas: 600 W. Alec Schenk, Nick Fluellen, Bard Hoover and John McGregor, investment specialists in Marcus & Millichap’s Dallas office, exclusively marketed the property on behalf of the seller, a Texas-based private client and procured the buyer, a California-based real estate investment firm. stories.title: Cerity Partners Expands to 68K SF at Global Holdings’ 99 Park Avenue
stories.excerpt: Wealth management firm Cerity Partners is expanding its offices at Midtown’s 99 Park Avenue. The tenant, which just expanded to 48,671 square feet at the building in December, has signed a deal for 19,600 additional square feet on the eighth floor of Global Holdings’ 26-story office building, bringing its total footprint to about 68,300 square feet, according to the landlord. It was a 15-year deal with an asking rent starting at $90 per square foot, Global Holdings confirmed. At least some of the space Cerity occupies is on a sublease, however, as the firm had been a subtenant on the 16th floor of 99 Park Avenue since at least 2024. Cerity will transition to direct occupancy next year. Global Holdings’ Alexander Radmin represented the landlord in-house alongside JLL’s Paul Glickman, Diana Biasotti, Kristen Morgan and Harrison Potter, while a Cushman & Wakefield team of Nicholas Dysenchuk and Rob Lowe negotiated on behalf of Cerity Partners. JLL and C&W did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Crain’s New York Business first reported the deal. Other tenants in the 600,000-square-foot building include Nashville-based real estate development firm Southern Land Company, which signed a 13,000-square-foot lease in June 2025. That deal brought the building to full occupancy. But that may have changed when health care products company On The Right Track Systems signed a 4,157-square-foot relocation deal at Olmstead Properties’ 381 Park Avenue South, Commercial Observer reported in August. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Cerity Partners expanded Midtown office to 68,300 sf total; 19,600 sf additional on floor 8

stories.summary: Wealth management firm Cerity Partners signed a 15-year, 19,600-sf expansion at Global Holdings' 99 Park Avenue in Midtown Manhattan, bringing total footprint to 68,300 sf at $90/sf asking rent. Cerity had been a subtenant since 2024 and will transition to direct occupancy in 2027. The deal demonstrates tenant stability and confidence in Midtown office demand.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily relevance. However, expanding high-revenue professional services presence in Midtown signals ongoing white-collar workforce concentration in Manhattan, supporting continued rental demand in Midtown South and East side multifamily corridors, particularly among young professionals and executives.

stories.title: Talonvest Arranges $63M for Bethesda Self-Storage Property
stories.excerpt: Talonvest Capital, a commercial real estate advisory firm, has secured a $63 million bridge loan on behalf of 1784 Holdings, a privately held real estate development company specializing in the development, construction, and operation of self-storage facilities. The loan, totaling $63 million, is a pre–Certificate of Occupancy bridge financing for a Class A self-storage facility in Bethesda, Maryland. Talonvest’s Thomas Sherlock, Kim Bishop, Mason Brusseau, and Lauren Maehler arranged the financing. The facility will comprise 1,560 climate-controlled units totaling 131,559 square feet. The property is strategically located along River Road in an affluent Washington, D.C.-area submarket seven miles from the U.S. Capitol. Talonvest secured the bridge loan with a four-year term, full-term interest-only payments, and an extension option from a private credit lender. “Talonvest has been a valuable partner in supporting our continued growth,” said Shane Albers, CEO and Principal of 1784 Holdings. “Their team understands our business, approaches each financing strategically, and consistently delivers solutions that align with our objectives.” The post Talonvest Arranges $63M for Bethesda Self-Storage Property appeared first on Connect CRE.

stories.summary: Talonvest Capital secured a $63 million pre-Certificate of Occupancy bridge loan from a private credit lender for 1784 Holdings' Class A self-storage facility in Bethesda, Maryland. The 1,560-unit, 131,559-sf property is located on River Road in an affluent Washington, D.C. submarket seven miles from the Capitol. The loan features a four-year term with full interest-only payments.

stories.title: Darwin Investment Group Completes $130M Refinance of Industrial Portfolio
stories.excerpt: Darwin Investment Group announced the completion of a $130 million refinancing of a 39-building industrial portfolio totaling more than 2 million square feet across the greater Chicago area and Southeast Wisconsin. The financing was provided by a dedicated Middle Market Real Estate team within Wells Fargo Commercial Banking. In conjunction with the refinancing, Darwin Investment Group principals George Cibula and Matthew Lewandowski acquired the 49% ownership interest held by their partners, bringing their ownership of the 39-building portfolio to 100%. The refinancing and ownership consolidation were facilitated on behalf of Darwin Investment Group by Matthew Lewandowski, Erin Cibula and Patricia Liston, working closely with Wells Fargo Commercial Banking’s Middle Market Real Estate team to complete the transaction. The Wells Fargo deal team was led by Commercial Banking Leader Paul Mokhatas, Senior Relationship Manager Anu Agarwal, and Portfolio Management Manager Paul Crusen. The portfolio consists of properties extending from Chicago’s south suburbs through Southeast Wisconsin and is home to more than 225 tenants. The post Darwin Investment Group Completes $130M Refinance of Industrial Portfolio appeared first on Connect CRE.

stories.title: Get to Know the Broker: Lauren Muss of Douglas Elliman
stories.excerpt: Lauren Muss has made a name for herself as an expert in the real estate industry, fueled by determination and grit. After running her own high-end accessory company — where, as a trained gemologist, she sold her products nationally — the native New Yorker joined the real estate business in 1994 and now works as an agent at Douglas Elliman. She has achieved over $7 billion in sales across some of Manhattan’s most prominent neighborhoods. But, at the beginning of her career, Muss wasn’t sure what her next move should be. She asked her friends if she should get her license and go into real estate. They said yes, and she did. “I started with my first listing for $400,000 and had an open house every weekend,” Muss said. “It was like the Fabergé ad for those who are old enough to remember. Those people told two friends, and then those people told two friends, and voila — I was in business.” Commercial Observer caught up with Muss in September for a series called “Get to Know the Broker,” where we connect with residential brokers to learn more about what makes them tick. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Commercial Observer: What has been the biggest deal of your career so far? Lauren Muss: I have sold a few penthouses in the $40 million to $50 million range at the Pierre, 160 Leroy Street, the Baccarat and 33 East 74th Street. This year alone, I’ve sold a few townhouses, units at the Surrey, 70 Vestry, 200 East 79th Street, and in a new developments in the $20 million range. What is your career Everest? I think I’ve actually reached my most ambitious goal: building a team of seven professionals, each with 12 to 23 years in the business, who work with me rather than for me. Clients can work directly alongside any of them, not just me. I have no assistants, everyone is trained to work the way I learned, with full ownership over what they handle. stories.title: The Power of the Public-Private Partnership for Affordable Housing
stories.excerpt: Without access to a safe, stable and affordable place to live, people lack the foundation for financial, physical and emotional well-being. Yet, right now, far too many Americans are struggling to find homes they can afford, and, as costs continue to rise, the challenge becomes more acute. According to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, the United States remains 4.7 million homes short and nearly a third of households are cost burdened. Twenty-six states have fewer than 4.7 million people. This housing trajectory, if continued, will prove ruinous for the American economy. Housing is foundational to financial, physical and emotional well-being, but the path to solving the housing crisis is not one-dimensional. It requires understanding where existing models have fallen short — and building a better framework from there. Two models have defined American affordable housing for a generation. We’re seeing the failures of both systems play out in real time. Will Blodgett. PHOTO: Axel Dupeux/for Commercial Observer The public housing authorities that oversee some of the country’s biggest affordable portfolios often face significant challenges in keeping pace with repairs, modernization and expansion. This is not a criticism of these essential institutions, but rather an acknowledgement of the structural constraints under which they operate. While working at the New York City Housing Authority, the country’s largest housing authority, I saw firsthand that operating roughly 177,000 apartments on a limited budget within a massive bureaucracy is extraordinarily difficult and there’s no easy answer. The private real estate sector is motivated primarily by market dynamics, which can mean mass displacement when affordability agreements expire and rents rise. Private capital, meanwhile, excels at mobilizing resources, managing risk, and executing projects at scale. stories.title: Virginia, Maryland Tighten Data Center Rules as Scrutiny Intensifies
stories.excerpt: Data center development will face tighter regulations across the Mid-Atlantic after officials in Virginia and Maryland unveiled new frameworks to corral the intense growth. Maryland Gov. Wes Moore on Wednesday announced an executive order establishing a review process for data centers of 25 megawatts or more whenever developers seek state permits, incentives or letters of support. The order also creates a task force that will evaluate projects based on their effects on ratepayers and the grid. The governor said local officials will still decide whether projects can ultimately move forward. Projects that do not align with the new framework can face deferred state review and will not be eligible for state advocacy or certain incentives. Moore also said his administration will seek to repeal Maryland’s sales and use tax exemption that was enacted in 2020. That followed a day after the Prince William County Board of County Supervisors in Virginia unanimously approved changes that largely end by-right data center development. The county — which is one of the country’s largest data center markets — is set to shrink its Data Center Opportunity Zone Overlay District from 9,698 acres to roughly 3,641 acres, and new proposals outside the overlay must proceed through a special-use permit process. Prince William created the overlay in 2016 to encourage data center development near high-voltage transmission lines. Prince William’s own planning documents describe the zoning amendment as a structural shift from the previous approach in how the county approves new data centers. And, last week, Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger announced a broad “Data Center Accountability Framework” and signed Executive Order 22, immediately directing state agencies to increase transparency, environmental oversight and scrutiny of the data center industry. Separately, her administration is proposing legislation for the 2027 legislative session that would eliminate by-right approval for data centers
bullets: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore issued executive order requiring review of data centers 25+ megawatts; task force to evaluate grid impact
Maryland repealing 2020 sales/use tax exemption for data centers; Prince William County, Virginia tightened approval process

stories.summary: Maryland Governor Wes Moore announced an executive order establishing a mandatory review process for data center projects of 25+ megawatts seeking state permits, incentives, or advocacy. A state task force will evaluate grid and ratepayer impacts; local approval still required. Maryland also plans to repeal its 2020 sales and use tax exemption for data centers. Virginia's Prince William County simultaneously tightened data center approval processes.
stories.impact: Regulatory restrictions on data center development in Mid-Atlantic slow large-facility growth that would typically attract job-creating corporate tenants and migrating workforces. Tightened permitting and incentive withdrawal reduce multifamily demand tailwinds that data center ecosystems normally generate (e.g., tech worker in-migration, wage growth, household formation). Developers should reassess multifamily underwriting in Virginia and Maryland submarkets previously benefiting from data center cluster dynamics; alternative job growth drivers (biotech, government, professional services) will dominate.
